slides.1.highlights.0.title: Lead with the core

slides.1.highlights.1.title: Answer frame
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Region questions: location and climate → main grapes → key rules → typical producers or style; spirit questions: raw material → distillation → maturation → rules
slides.1.highlights.2.title: When unsure
slides.1.highlights.2.content: State what you are sure of and flag what you are not; better than guessing a precise number, and the same honesty valued in MW and Diploma work
slides.1.content: Fast, accurate, complete: an oral exam shows the structure of your knowledge in a short time.

Oral question: name the five protected Scotch regions and give one style trait for each.
Highland: the largest, with varied styles
Lowland: often lighter and delicate
Speyside: the densest cluster of distilleries, often fruity or sherry-cask styles
Islay: peat smoke
Campbeltown: few distilleries, often briny and oily

Highland (the largest, varied styles), Lowland (often lighter and delicate), Speyside (the densest cluster of distilleries, often fruity or sherry-cask styles), Islay (peat smoke), Campbeltown (few distilleries, often briny and oily). These are common tendencies; distilleries vary widely.
Oral question: compare junmai daiginjo and honjozo in ingredients, polishing and style.
Junmai daiginjo: only rice, koji and water, no added alcohol
Junmai daiginjo: polishing ratio 50% or less
Honjozo: may add a little brewer’s alcohol, polishing 70% or less
Style: daiginjo is fragrant and usually chilled; honjozo is lighter and can be warmed

Junmai daiginjo uses only rice, koji and water, polished to 50% or less; it is fragrant and refined and usually served chilled. Honjozo is polished to 70% or less and may include a little brewer’s alcohol for a fresher aroma and lighter palate; it is affordable and suits warming. Added alcohol is a style choice, not a sign of lower quality.
Oral question: describe the main rules for Bourbon and explain how new charred barrels affect its style.
At least 51% corn
Matured in new charred oak containers
Distilled to ≤80%, barrelled at ≤62.5%, bottled at ≥40%
Straight Bourbon at least 2 years
New charred barrels → rich vanilla, caramel and sweetness, faster maturation

Bourbon needs at least 51% corn, maturation in new charred oak containers, distillation to no more than 80%, barrelling at no more than 62.5% and bottling at least 40%; Straight Bourbon needs at least 2 years. New charred barrels extract strongly, and the caramelised wood sugars of the char give rich vanilla, caramel and sweetness; with Kentucky’s climate, maturation is faster than in Scotland.
